title: A boy's lunch (John 6:1–14)
hookLine: five loaves and two fish from a child, and five thousand eat with baskets left over

lines: A HUNGRY CROWD ON A HILLSIDE.
cards: Not enough money for the month. Not enough time. Not enough patience for the kids tonight.
Some sums never add up. Here's one on a grassy hillside by the Sea of Galilee. A huge crowd has followed Jesus there, because they've seen him heal the sick.
Thousands of them, and nothing to eat. Jesus turns to one of his disciples, Philip, and asks a question John says was a test: where are we going to buy bread for all these people?

teach.h: TWO HUNDRED DAYS' WAGES, NOT ENOUGH.
teach.b: Philip does the math, in the King James Bible: "Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them, that every one of them may take a little."
A penny there is a denarius, a laborer's day's wage in one of Jesus's parables: two hundred days' wages, and still not a bite each.

Then Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, comes back with something almost funny: "There is a lad here, which hath five barley loaves, and two small fishes: but what are they among so many?" Only John mentions the boy.
Barley, some readers point out, was the cheaper grain. This is a kid's packed lunch, and somebody has to hand it over. Jesus has the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men, John says.

He takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. Then a quieter line: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers.
Twelve, from five loaves. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell this feeding too; it's in all four Gospels.
Christians read it as a wonder, and some also hear in it the table of communion: he takes bread, gives thanks, and gives it.
Later in the chapter he calls himself the bread of life.
But start with the boy. Nobody asks him to fix the problem. He offers what he has, small as it is, and it turns out to be enough, with baskets to spare.

how: Many churches read the feeding of the five thousand alongside teaching about communion and about sharing with people in need. Some church meals and food programs point to this story.

games.why: Andrew brings it: there is a lad here, but what are they among so many? it was enough, with twelve baskets over.

practice: Think of a need you know about right now, a struggling friend, a cause you care about, a tired colleague, a lonely family member.
Instead of everything it would take, look at what you actually have, ten minutes, a skill, a spare meal, a kind word, your five loaves and two fish, and picture handing it over.
If you pray, you can give thanks for it first, the way he did.
